channel.title: Thirsty Planet
channel.description: Understanding water, before it's gone. The hidden water inside everyday things, the water industry in plain words, and the places already solving it.

item.title: Thirsty: Tea
item.description:
A cup of tea carries about 27 litres of water. A cup of coffee carries about 140. The two drinks are made the same way, from the leaves or seeds of a tropical shrub, and the difference is mostly how much of the plant goes into the cup.
Tea, by the Water Footprint Network's method, comes to about 8,900 litres per kilogram of made tea, half of coffee's figure per kilogram. A cup uses two or three grams of leaf where a cup of coffee uses seven of beans, and the arithmetic does the rest.
The leaf grows where it rains. Assam, Darjeeling, the highlands of Sri Lanka and Kenya, the hills of southern China: all of them are places of heavy monsoon or highland rain, and tea's footprint is overwhelmingly green. Processing the leaf, withering, rolling, oxidising and drying, uses almost no water at all.
It is one of the gentler things in a kitchen, in water terms, and one of the few in this series where the number is small, the water is rain, and the place could spare it.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Sugar
item.description:
A kilogram of cane sugar carries about 1,782 litres of water. A kilogram of beet sugar carries about half that. The two are chemically identical in the bag, and the difference is the plant and the place.
Sugar cane is a tropical grass that grows for a year or more and drinks all of it. Sugar beet is a temperate root that grows for one summer on rain. Cane is most of the world's sugar, and where it is grown decides everything: in Brazil, the largest producer, it is mostly rain fed; in India, the second, it is irrigated, and in Maharashtra cane takes the majority of the state's irrigation water on a small fraction of its farmland.
The mill has a story too. Crushing cane and refining sugar uses little water in the product, but the distilleries that turn cane molasses into ethanol produce spent wash, the strongest effluent on the water industry's scale, a hundred times raw sewage.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Smartphone
item.description:
A smartphone took about 12,760 litres of water to make, by the estimate Friends of the Earth published in 2015, which remains one of the few that shows its working. That is more than a pair of jeans, and the phone weighs 170 grams.
Almost none of that water is where people expect. The mine for the metals is a small share. The largest share is in the semiconductor plant that made the chips, where a silicon wafer is rinsed hundreds of times in water so pure that it would pull the minerals out of your body if you drank it. Making that water, and cleaning what comes back, is the plant's biggest water job. A large chip factory uses as much water as a town.
The rest is spread across the screen, the battery, the circuit board and the metals, each with its own rinse. What the number says is simple: the water in a phone is industrial water, in a handful of factories in East Asia, and the way to make a phone thirsty is to buy a new one every two years.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Pork
item.description:
A kilogram of pork carries about 6,000 litres of water in the global averages. That puts it between chicken, at about 4,300, and beef, at over 15,000, and the reason is the same as for both: feed.
A pig eats about three kilograms of feed for every kilogram it gains, mostly maize, wheat, barley and soy, and the water in the pork is the rain and irrigation that grew those crops. The pig itself drinks a few litres a day and is washed with a few more. Nine tenths of the number was spent on a field, often on another continent.
What makes pork different is the manure. A pig produces several times its own weight in slurry over its life, the slurry is stored in open lagoons and sprayed on fields, and where the pigs are dense, in eastern North Carolina, in Brittany, in the Netherlands, in the provinces of eastern China, the fields cannot take it and the rivers show it. The water footprint puts that as grey water. The people downstream call it something else.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Windhoek
item.description:
Every article about water reuse eventually mentions Singapore. The city that did it first, and did it more directly than anyone has since, is Windhoek, the capital of Namibia, and it started in 1968.
Namibia is the driest country in sub Saharan Africa, and Windhoek sits in the middle of it, far from any river, on an aquifer that was running low by the 1950s. With the town growing and no new source within reach, its engineers did the thing that every other city has avoided: they built a plant that takes the treated effluent from the sewage works and, after a further chain of treatment, puts it straight into the drinking water mains. No reservoir in between, no river, no aquifer. Direct potable reuse, the industry calls it, and Windhoek has run it for more than fifty years.
The plant has been rebuilt twice and supplies up to about a third of the city's drinking water. There has never been a recorded outbreak of illness traced to it. The rest of the world took half a century to follow, and the reasons say more about trust than about engineering.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Tehran
item.description:
Tehran sits under the Alborz mountains, and for a century the snow on those mountains was its water, held in five dams on the rivers that come down from them and drawn from an aquifer under the plain. In the drought that began around 2018 and deepened through 2025, the dams fell to under a fifth of their capacity, the city cut its pressure, and the government spoke, for the first time, of rationing by district and of moving the capital.
The drought is real and the climate is drying. The larger cause is what Iran has done with its water for fifty years: dammed nearly every river, pumped its aquifers to grow wheat and rice in the desert in the name of self sufficiency, and drained Lake Urmia, once the largest lake in the Middle East, to a salt flat. Tehran's own plain has sunk by up to a quarter of a metre a year in the south west as its wells are pumped, cracking the pipes and the runways of the airport.
What the city can still do is the list this series always arrives at: reuse its sewage, mend its pipes, price the water, and stop farming the desert with the aquifer. What it has done is announce another dam.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: São Paulo
item.description:
São Paulo is a city of twenty million people in one of the wettest countries on Earth, and in 2014 it nearly ran out of water. The Cantareira system, which supplied nearly half the city, fell below the level of its intakes, and the utility installed pumps to draw the dead volume from the bottom of the reservoirs. By early 2015 even that was down to about five percent.
The rain had failed for two summers, the worst drought in the region's recorded history, and the failure landed on a system that had no margin. The city had grown, the reservoirs had not, a quarter of the water leaked from the pipes, and the forests of the Cantareira hills, which held the rain and released it slowly, had mostly been cleared for pasture. The utility cut pressure at night, offered discounts for saving, and denied for months that rationing was coming, while whole neighbourhoods went without water for days at a time.
The rains came back in 2015 and 2016. What was built afterwards, a new reservoir link, a leak programme, and payments to farmers to replant the hills, is the plan the city should have had before.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Phoenix
item.description:
Phoenix is the fastest growing large city in the United States and it is in the Sonoran Desert, with two hundred millimetres of rain, summers at fifty degrees, and a river, the Salt, that has not flowed through the city since it was dammed a century ago. Its water is a canal, an aquifer, and a law.
The canal is the Central Arizona Project, 541 kilometres from the Colorado River at Lake Havasu, lifting the water nearly nine hundred metres across the desert to Phoenix and Tucson. It opened in the 1990s and it holds the most junior right on the river, which means that when the Colorado is cut, as it was in 2022 and 2023, Arizona is cut first and most. The law is the Groundwater Management Act of 1980, which requires any new subdivision in the valley to prove a hundred years of water before it is built, and which, in 2023, the state used to stop new housing on groundwater across parts of the metropolitan area.
It is a city that has, unusually, written its limits down. What it has not done is decide what happens when the canal delivers less, and that decision is arriving.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Orange County
item.description:
The largest water reuse plant in the world is in Orange County, California, and it was built because of the sea.
The county's two and a half million people drink from an aquifer under the coastal plain, and by the 1970s they had pumped it so hard that seawater was creeping inland through the sand and salting the wells. The first answer, in 1976, was to inject treated wastewater along the coast as a wall of fresh water to push the sea back. The second, in 2008, was the Groundwater Replenishment System: sewage effluent through microfiltration, reverse osmosis and ultraviolet light, then into the barrier and into recharge basins inland, where it soaks down into the aquifer and comes up, months later, through the county's wells.
It has been expanded twice and now makes 130 million gallons a day, about 490,000 cubic metres, enough for a million people. Everyone in the county drinks it. Almost nobody thinks about it, which was the point of the fifteen years of public work that preceded it, learned from San Diego, next door, where the same plant was proposed a decade earlier and killed by three words.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: The Murray Darling
item.description:
The Murray Darling Basin is a seventh of Australia, it grows about 40 percent of the country's food, and for most of the twentieth century its rivers were shared out among four states on the assumption that there would always be enough. There was not. By the 2000s the Murray no longer reached the sea without dredging, the lakes at its mouth were turning acid, and a drought that lasted a decade emptied the storages.
The country's answer, in 2012, was a plan that set a limit on how much could be taken and undertook to return 2,750 billion litres a year to the rivers, by buying water rights from farmers on an open market and by paying for irrigation works that use less. It is the largest water market on Earth, and the largest deliberate transfer of water from farms to a river anywhere.
A decade on, most of the water has been recovered, the mouth is open, and the fights have moved to the last few hundred gigalitres, to the floodplain forests that still do not flood, and to the million fish that died in the Darling in 2019. It is a partial success, which in this series counts as a success.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Mexico City
item.description:
Mexico City was a lake. The Aztecs built their capital on an island in it, the Spanish drained it over three centuries, and twenty two million people now live on the soft clay of the old lake bed. The city takes most of its water from the aquifer under that clay, and as the water is pumped out the clay compacts, and the city sinks. In places it is sinking by up to fifty centimetres a year. The cathedral leans. The metro tunnels bend. Pipes crack, and about forty percent of the water in them leaks out before it reaches a tap.
The rest of the water comes from the Cutzamala system, a chain of reservoirs a hundred kilometres away that pumps water up more than a thousand metres over the mountains and into the valley, at a cost in electricity that is one of the largest single power bills in the country. In 2024, after a dry year, the Cutzamala reservoirs fell to under a third and the city talked about its own Day Zero.
What makes Mexico City different from the other places in this series is inequality. The wealthy west has water twenty four hours a day. The eastern districts have it a few hours a week and buy the rest from tankers. The engineering problem and the political one are the same problem.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Lima
item.description:
Lima gets about nine millimetres of rain a year. It is the second largest city in the world built on a desert, after Cairo, and ten million people live there on a river, the Rímac, that comes down from the Andes carrying the melt of glaciers that have lost a large share of their ice in fifty years.
The water reaches most of the city through pipes, treated at a plant on the river's edge. It does not reach the hills. A million and a half people in the settlements that climb the dry slopes around the city have no connection, and they buy water from tanker trucks at a price per litre that is ten times what a household in the wealthy districts pays for a piped supply, for water that is dirtier and stored in a drum on the roof.
The city's future is a set of hard choices: reservoirs high in the Andes to replace the glaciers, a tunnel through the mountains from the wet side, treated sewage for the parks and the farms, and the slow work of laying pipes up the hills. On the hills themselves, a few communities have found that the fog that rolls in off the Pacific can be caught in nets. It is a small amount of water. It is theirs.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Las Vegas
item.description:
Las Vegas is the city everyone names as the waste of water in the desert, and it is one of the most water efficient cities in the United States. Both reputations come from the Strip.
The facts are these. Nevada has the smallest share of the Colorado River of any state, 300,000 acre feet a year, about 370 million cubic metres, and Las Vegas takes ninety percent of its water from it, through Lake Mead. Since 2002 the city's population has grown by about half and its use of the river has fallen by about a quarter. Nearly all water used indoors, in every hotel, casino and home, goes to a treatment plant and back into the lake, and the city gets a credit for every litre returned. The fountains at the Bellagio run on that returned water and on an old well under the hotel.
What is actually lost is water sprayed on grass, which evaporates and never returns. So the city paid residents to tear out lawns, more than 200 million square feet of them, and in 2021 Nevada passed a law banning ornamental turf in the valley outright, the first such law in the country. The lesson is the plainest in this series: measure what leaves, and go after that.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Jakarta
item.description:
Jakarta is sinking. In its northern districts the ground is going down by up to twenty five centimetres a year, faster than in any other large city, and about two fifths of the city already lies below sea level, behind walls that the sea has breached more than once. The cause is under the streets: ten million people, and the factories and malls among them, pumping the aquifer for water that the pipes do not bring.
Only about two thirds of the city is connected to piped water, the supply is unreliable, and so nearly every building has a well. As the water is drawn out, the soft delta sediment compacts and the surface drops, taking the roads, the drains and the flood walls with it. The rivers that cross the city to the sea now have to be pumped uphill.
Indonesia's answer is to move the capital to Borneo, which relieves the government and leaves the ten million people where they are. The answer for them is the one this series keeps finding: pipes that deliver, so the wells can be shut, and a sea wall to buy the time to lay them.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Israel
item.description:
Israel is more than half desert, it grows most of its own food, and it exports fruit and vegetables to Europe in winter. Most of that comes down to two ideas from the 1960s, and both were about not wasting a drop.
The first is drip irrigation. A water engineer named Simcha Blass noticed a tree growing larger than its neighbours beside a leaking pipe, and worked out that water delivered slowly, at the root, grew more with less than water sprayed over a field. The first commercial drip system was made at Kibbutz Hatzerim in the Negev in 1965, and the company that grew from it, Netafim, now sells it on every continent. A drip line puts water where the plant is and nowhere else, and it roughly halves what a crop needs.
The second is reuse. The treated sewage of Tel Aviv goes to the Negev rather than to the sea, filtered through the sand of the coastal aquifer and piped south to irrigate the Negev, and the country reuses a larger share of its wastewater for farming than any other. Add five desalination plants on the coast, and a nation with no water to spare has water to sell.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Chennai
item.description:
In June 2019 Chennai's four reservoirs held about a tenth of one percent of their capacity. The city of ten million people declared Day Zero, offices sent staff home, restaurants closed, and the state began running trains of fifty wagons, 2.5 million litres each, from a river two hundred kilometres away.
Chennai gets more rain than London. It gets it in about six weeks, from the north east monsoon in November and December, and in 2015 that monsoon put the city under two metres of water. The problem was never the amount of rain. It was that the city had built over the lakes and marshes that once held it, that the monsoon failed three years running, and that the groundwater under every neighbourhood had been pumped out by borewells to make up the difference.
What is instructive is what came before and after. Tamil Nadu made rainwater harvesting compulsory on every building in 2003, and the structures on the roofs are why the aquifer recovered as fast as it did when the rain came back. Two desalination plants supplied a fifth of the city through the crisis, and two more are being built. The trains were the emergency. The barrels and the plants are the plan.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Cape Town
item.description:
In the summer of 2018 Cape Town came within weeks of being the first major city in the modern world to switch off its water supply, and it did not, and the reasons are more useful than the drama.
Three dry winters in a row took the city's dams from full to a fifth. The city, late, imposed a limit of 50 litres per person per day, cut the pressure in the pipes, published its dam levels weekly, and mapped the collection points where the army would hand out 25 litres a head. Cape Town's households cut the city's consumption by more than half, mostly in their bathrooms, and pushed the projected date back until the winter rain arrived in June.
Since then the city has drilled into its aquifers, built small desalination plants, started reusing treated wastewater, and rebuilt its planning around a drought of four years rather than two. The dams refilled. The habits, partly, stayed.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Beijing
item.description:
Beijing has about a hundred cubic metres of water per person a year, a tenth of what the United Nations calls scarcity, less than Saudi Arabia, and twenty two million people. For four decades it drank the aquifer under the North China Plain, and the water table fell by a metre a year and the ground with it.
In 2014 China finished the largest water transfer ever built. The central route of the South to North Water Transfer takes water from a reservoir on the Han River, a tributary of the Yangtze, and carries it 1,432 kilometres north in an open canal, by gravity, over and under rivers and railways, to Beijing and Tianjin. Beijing now takes about two thirds of its tap water from it, the water table has begun to rise, and the city's reservoirs have refilled for the first time in a generation.
It cost tens of billions of dollars, moved several hundred thousand people from the reservoir's shore, and takes a river's water from the people who lived on it. It has also worked, which is more than most of the projects in this series can say, and it has bought the city time rather than water. The city still uses more than it has.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: The Aral Sea
item.description:
In 1960 the Aral Sea, on the border of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was the fourth largest lake in the world, with a fishing fleet that landed tens of thousands of tonnes a year. By 2010 about ninety percent of its water was gone, its fishing ports stood a hundred kilometres from the shore, and the seabed had become a desert with a name, the Aralkum, whose salt and pesticide dust blows across the region.
It was drained on purpose. From the 1960s the two rivers that fed it, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, were diverted through thousands of kilometres of canals to grow cotton across the deserts of Soviet Central Asia. The plan worked, in its own terms. Uzbekistan became a cotton giant. The sea shrank as the plan intended, and nobody in charge stopped it.
One part has come back. A dam finished in 2005 across the narrow channel to the northern basin has refilled it, and fish and fishermen have returned to Aralsk. The larger southern basin is gone for good. The t-shirt article on this site mentioned the sea. This one goes there.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Leather shoes
item.description:
A pair of leather shoes carries about 8,000 litres of water, about the same as a pair of jeans, and almost none of it was used at the tannery.
Leather is a by product of beef. The hide is a few percent of an animal's value, and the footprint method gives it a few percent of the animal's water, which is three years of feed. Bovine leather comes to about 17,000 litres per kilogram by the Water Footprint Network's method, and a pair of shoes uses roughly half a kilo of it. That is where the 8,000 comes from, and, as with the steak, nearly all of it is rain on pasture and feed crops.
The tannery's share is small in volume and large in trouble. Turning a raw hide into leather takes 15 to 40 cubic metres of water per tonne of hides, and what leaves carries salt, lime, sulphide, chromium and an organic load that a river cannot take. It is one of the hardest effluents in industry, and the tanning clusters of India and Bangladesh are where I first saw what it does.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Steel
item.description:
A tonne of steel takes about 28,000 litres of water through the works and keeps about 3,300 of them, by the industry's own survey. The rest goes back to the river, warmer and, at a well run plant, cleaner than it came. The world makes two billion tonnes a year, so the consumption comes to several cubic kilometres and the withdrawal to twenty times that.
Almost all of it is cooling. A blast furnace, a basic oxygen converter, a continuous caster and a hot rolling mill are each machines for handling metal at over a thousand degrees, and every one of them is cooled by water running through its walls, rolls and hearths. The rest quenches red hot coke and slag, scrubs the dust out of furnace gas, and descales the slab under the rolls. The water that is consumed is what evaporates from the cooling towers and the quench.
The industry is changing, and the water will change with it. Steel from scrap in an electric furnace uses a fraction of the water of steel from ore in a blast furnace, and steel from hydrogen and iron ore, which the industry is building to cut its carbon, will consume more water at the electrolysis than it saves at the coke ovens. It is a water story told in the shape of a furnace.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Power Stations
item.description:
The largest user of fresh water in the United States is power stations, ahead of farming. About 41 percent of all the fresh water withdrawn in the country goes to cooling them, according to the national survey, ahead of irrigation, and the same is true in much of Europe.
The reason is steam. A coal, gas or nuclear plant boils water to spin a turbine, and the steam has to be condensed back to water to be boiled again. Condensing it takes a river of cooling water: a large plant on a once through system draws a hundred thousand litres for every megawatt hour it makes and returns nearly all of it, warmer. A plant with cooling towers draws far less and evaporates most of what it draws, about 2,500 litres a megawatt hour, which is gone.
The number is moving. Wind and solar use almost no water, gas plants use less than coal, and in the summer of 2022 France turned down reactors because the Rhône was too warm to take their heat. The grid is becoming less thirsty by the year, and the reason has nothing to do with water policy: the thirsty plants are closing.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Leather and tanning
item.description:
Of all the industries in this series, tanning is the one whose water frightens treatment engineers most, and it is the oldest of them all.
A tannery turns a raw hide, which would rot in days, into leather, which lasts decades, through a chain of baths: salt soaked out, hair and flesh removed with lime and sulphide, the hide pickled in acid and tanned with chromium. Every bath goes to the drain, and what leaves carries salt, lime, sulphide, chromium and an organic load of hair, flesh and blood many times that of sewage. It is the textile effluent with metals and poison gas added.
The industry moved, over fifty years, from Europe to the countries with the hides and the labour, and the damage moved with it. Kanpur on the Ganges, Hazaribagh in Dhaka, Ranipet in Tamil Nadu, Fez in Morocco: rivers the colour of dye, chromium in the wells. In 2017 Bangladesh moved Dhaka's entire tanning district to a new estate with a common treatment plant. Whether the plant runs is the question I have gone to see.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Hydrogen
item.description:
Green hydrogen is made by running electricity through water. The chemistry is fixed: nine litres of water become one kilogram of hydrogen and eight kilograms of oxygen. In practice a plant uses two to three times that, for cooling and for purifying the water first, so a kilogram of hydrogen leaves the plant with twenty to thirty litres behind it.
That is a small number per kilogram and a large one per plant. The projects announced in Saudi Arabia, Oman, Namibia, Chile and Australia are sized in millions of tonnes a year, and a million tonnes of hydrogen means tens of millions of cubic metres of water, in places where the whole point is the desert sun. Nearly all of them will desalinate, which adds energy and a brine to the coast.
The water is manageable, and the industry knows it, and the plants are designed for it. What it does is make green hydrogen a coastal industry as much as a solar one, and it puts a new, very large water user next to the fishing towns and the desalination plants that were there first.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Data Centres
item.description:
Google's data centres consumed about 23 billion litres of water in 2023, by the company's own environmental report, up from about 21 billion the year before. Microsoft's use grew by a third in a single year. The reason is heat.
A rack of servers turns electricity into heat, all of it, and the heat has to go somewhere. The cheapest way to get rid of it is to evaporate water in a cooling tower, and the water that evaporates is gone from the river or the aquifer it came from. A large data centre can consume as much water as a town of tens of thousands of people, and the buildings are being put up in dry places, because dry places have cheap land and cheap power.
Artificial intelligence has made the numbers move. Training and running the large models takes far more computing per task than a search did, and one widely cited study put a chatbot's water at about half a litre for every twenty to fifty questions, once the cooling and the power station are counted. The industry is responding, with closed loop cooling and pledges to replenish more than it uses. Whether those pledges add up is the water question of the decade.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Copper
item.description:
A tonne of copper takes about seventy thousand litres of water to get out of the ground, at the average of the mines that publish their figures. The world uses about 26 million tonnes a year, and the transition to electric cars, wind turbines and grids will need something like twice that by the 2040s. About a quarter of it comes from Chile, and most of Chile's comes from the Atacama, the driest desert on Earth.
The water is in the mill. Copper ore is less than one percent metal, so a tonne of copper is a hundred tonnes of rock, crushed to powder and floated in tanks of water and chemicals where the copper minerals rise with the froth and the rock sinks. The wet waste goes to a tailings dam. For a century the mines of the Atacama drew that water from the aquifers under the salt flats, and the flats, the lagoons and the villages that shared them dried.
The industry has done what it had to. The largest mines now pump seawater up three thousand metres from the coast, desalinated or raw, and Chile's rules have forced the rest to follow. It is the clearest case in mining of a thirsty industry moving its water to the sea, and it was pushed there by a desert that ran out.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Concrete
item.description:
Concrete is the second most used substance on Earth. Only water is used more, and concrete is made of it. The world pours around thirty billion tonnes a year, and a study in 2018 put the water consumed in making it at about nine percent of global industrial water withdrawals, more than any other manufactured product.
The water is in three places. A cubic metre of concrete needs about 150 to 200 litres of water to mix, which reacts with the cement and stays in the slab. It needs several times that again to cure, sprayed or ponded on the surface for days so the cement hardens properly. And the aggregate, the sand and gravel that make up three quarters of the mix, is washed with water at the quarry, which is often the largest share of all.
What makes it a water story is where it happens. Concrete is poured where cities are growing, and the cities growing fastest are in India, the Gulf, Africa and dry parts of China, on the same aquifers the farms and the people draw on. A tower in a desert is built with local water, at a rate of about a swimming pool per floor.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Gold
item.description:
A gold ring weighs about five grams, and the mine that produced its gold used about 3,500 litres of water to do it, by the best global average published. Per kilogram of metal, gold is one of the thirstiest things on Earth: around 700,000 litres, because a tonne of ore yields a gram or two of gold and every tonne has to be crushed to flour and washed.
The washing is with cyanide. Gold dissolves in a weak cyanide solution, so the crushed rock is soaked in it, in tanks or in great heaps, the gold is pulled out of the liquid, and the wet, cyanide bearing rock, the tailings, is pumped to a dam. Tailings dams are among the largest structures humans build, and when one fails, as at Baia Mare in 2000 or Brumadinho in 2019, a river dies for a hundred kilometres.
The large mines have learned to recycle most of their water and to destroy the cyanide before it leaves. The small ones, the artisanal miners who produce a fifth of the world's gold, use mercury instead, in rivers, with their hands, and that is the worst water story in mining.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty: An egg
item.description:
One egg carries about 196 litres of water, and the hen drank almost none of it.
A laying hen eats around 110 grams of feed a day, mostly maize and soybean meal, and lays an egg most days. Grow all that grain, divide its water by the eggs, and an egg comes to about 3,300 litres per kilo, or 196 litres for a 60 gram egg, by the Water Footprint Network's method. Her own drinking water is a few percent of that.
The number that makes the egg interesting is the one per gram of protein. Eggs need about 29 litres for a gram of protein, close to milk, a third of pork and a quarter of beef. Among animal foods, the egg is one of the most efficient there is, and about four fifths of its water is rain on a field of grain.
As always, the field decides the rest. Maize irrigated in a dry region and soy grown on rain in Brazil carry very different water, and the carton does not say which the hen ate.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Chicken
item.description:
A kilogram of chicken carries about 4,325 litres of water in the global averages, against roughly 6,000 for pork and 15,400 for beef. It is the least thirsty meat by a wide margin, and the reason is arithmetic.
A broiler chicken reaches its slaughter weight in about six weeks on around 1.6 kilograms of feed for every kilogram it gains. A pig needs closer to three, a cow six or more. The feed is where the water is, in the maize and soy that were grown, mostly on rain, to fill the bird's ration. Less feed per kilogram means less water per kilogram, and chicken wins that sum against every other animal.
Two things people miss. The first is that 4,300 litres is still four times the water in a kilogram of wheat, because feeding grain to an animal always loses most of it. The second is the plant. A chicken processing plant uses twenty to thirty litres of water per bird for scalding, washing and chilling, and its effluent is one of the strongest in the food industry.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Cheese
item.description:
It takes about ten litres of milk to make a kilogram of hard cheese, and a litre of milk carries about a thousand litres of water. So a kilo of cheese should carry ten thousand. The Water Footprint Network's figure is about 3,200, and the difference is the most interesting thing about the number.
When milk is made into cheese, nine tenths of it becomes whey, and whey is a product too: dried into protein powder, fed to pigs, digested for gas. The footprint method splits the milk's water between the cheese and the whey in proportion to their value, and the cheese carries only its share. The water was all used. It is divided differently.
The rest of the story is the cow, as with milk and beef: 96 percent of the water grew the feed, and whether it was rain on pasture or a river in a dry valley depends on the farm. And the cheese plant has a water story of its own, in the brine bath where the cheese is salted and in the cleaning of every pipe the milk touched.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Almonds
item.description:
A single almond takes about twelve litres of irrigation water to grow in California, where four out of five of the world's almonds come from. A kilogram of shelled almonds, in the global averages, runs to around 16,000 litres, most of it pumped.
The reason is geography. Almonds need a mild wet winter and a long hot dry summer, and the Central Valley has exactly that, which means every drop the trees drink between April and September comes from a canal or a well. The orchards more than doubled in twenty years, to well over a million acres, and a tree cannot be fallowed in a drought the way a field of tomatoes can. So in the dry years the wells ran, the valley floor sank, and the almond became the villain of California's water story.
It is a crop with a high value per drop and a low tolerance for a dry year. Both are true at once, and that is the story.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: ZLD
item.description:
There is a kind of factory that has no outfall. Nothing liquid leaves it. Every drop of water it uses is recovered and used again, and everything that was dissolved in that water comes out at the end as a solid, in bags. The industry calls it zero liquid discharge, ZLD, and it is the answer to the question every membrane plant leaves behind: what to do with the brine.
The process is a chain. Treatment, then membranes, which recover most of the water and leave a brine. Then evaporators, which boil the brine down using recovered heat, and finally a crystalliser, which turns the last of it into salt. The water is all recovered. The salt is dry. The energy bill is the catch, because boiling water is the most expensive thing that can be done to it.
In January 2011 the Madras High Court ordered every dyeing unit in Tirupur, the knitwear capital of southern India, to close until it achieved zero liquid discharge, and a whole industrial town learned to run these plants. It was expensive, and it is the clearest demonstration anywhere that the technology works when somebody insists.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Plain Water: Ultrapure water
item.description:
Most of this series is about making water clean enough to drink. There is an industry that needs water far cleaner than that, so clean that drinking it would be unpleasant and piping it through steel would dissolve the steel.
It is called ultrapure water, and it is what a semiconductor plant rinses its silicon wafers in, what a pharmaceutical plant makes injections from, and what a power station boils in its turbines. In a chip fab a single dissolved ion or a particle a few nanometres across on a wafer is a ruined circuit, so the water has to have, as nearly as physics allows, nothing in it. The measure is electrical: pure water barely conducts, and ultrapure water is pushed to 18.2 megohm centimetres, the theoretical limit, at which there is almost nothing dissolved to carry a charge.
It is made from ordinary tap water by a chain that starts with the reverse osmosis of the desalination article and goes far past it: two passes of membranes, an electric field to strip the last ions, ultraviolet light to break down organic molecules, resin polishers, and filters finer than anything in a drinking water plant. The water arrives at the wafer purer than anything in nature.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Reverse osmosis
item.description:
Reverse osmosis is the process behind nearly every drop of desalinated or recycled water on Earth, and its name describes exactly what it is: nature's process, run backwards, by force.
Put salty water and fresh water either side of a membrane that lets only water through, and the fresh water flows towards the salt. That is osmosis, the same pull that moves water into a plant's roots. For seawater the pull is worth about 27 bar. To make water go the other way, out of the salt and through the membrane, a plant has to push harder than that, and seawater plants run their pumps at 55 to 80 bar. The pumps are where the energy goes.
What comes through is water with about 99 percent of the salt removed. What stays behind is a brine, half the volume and twice the salt, and where that goes is the hardest question in the business.
Thirty years ago a seawater plant used around 8 kilowatt hours for every cubic metre. Today the best run at about 3. The membranes got better and, above all, the pressure in the brine is now recovered rather than thrown away. It is one of the quieter engineering successes of the age.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Phosphorus
item.description:
Nitrogen, the subject of the last article, can be sent back to the air, because that is where it came from. Phosphorus cannot. It came from rock, mined in a handful of countries, and once it has passed through a crop, a person and a sewer it is either in the sea or in the sludge at the back of the treatment plant.
Phosphorus in a lake grows algae, and in freshwater it is usually the nutrient that decides how much. Lake Erie turned green in the 1960s on phosphorus from detergents and sewage, and recovered when both were controlled. Sewage works now precipitate phosphorus out with iron or aluminium, or use bacteria that hoard it, and the limits have fallen to around a milligram per litre from the eight that arrives.
The interesting part is where it goes. The phosphate rock the world's fertiliser comes from is concentrated in Morocco above all, and it is finite. A city's sewage contains a large share of the phosphorus its food arrived with, and the plants that recover it as a crystal called struvite are, in a small way, mining their own sludge.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: pH
item.description:
Of all the numbers on a water report, pH is the one everyone half remembers from school and the one a plant operator checks first.
It measures how acid or alkaline water is, on a scale from 0 to 14 where 7 is neutral. The scale is logarithmic, so each step is ten times the last: water at pH 5 is ten times more acid than water at pH 6 and a hundred times more than at 7. Rain sits near 5.6, tap water between 6.5 and 8.5, seawater at about 8.1. A dye house's effluent leaves at 10 or 11, which is why the first thing an effluent plant does is neutralise it.
pH decides almost everything downstream. Fish sicken outside a narrow band. The bacteria that clean water in a treatment plant stop eating outside theirs. Coagulants only work in their window. And water that is slightly acid dissolves the pipes it flows through, which is how Flint, Michigan poisoned its children with lead in 2014: the city changed its water source and stopped adding the chemical that kept the pipes' lining intact.
One number, checked first, for good reason. The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: PFAS
item.description:
In 2024 the United States set its first national limit for two chemicals in drinking water at four nanograms per litre. Four parts per trillion. That is a single drop in twenty Olympic swimming pools, and it is the strictest drinking water limit ever set for anything.
The chemicals are PFOA and PFOS, the best known members of a family called PFAS, made since the 1940s for anything that needed to shed water or grease: non stick pans, waterproof jackets, food packaging, firefighting foam. The carbon fluorine bond that makes them useful makes them indestructible. They do not rot, burn or break down in sunlight. Every one made is still here, and they are in the blood of nearly every person tested.
They got into water from factories, from the foam used at airports and military bases, and from sewage sludge spread on fields. Getting them out is possible, with activated carbon, ion exchange resin or reverse osmosis, and it is expensive, and the industry that I work in has spent the last five years learning to do it. The chemicals themselves still have to go somewhere. That part is unsolved.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Nitrogen
item.description:
Every sewage works receives about 40 milligrams of nitrogen in every litre, nearly all of it as ammonia, nearly all of it from urine, and for most of the twentieth century it was let straight through to the river.
Nitrogen in a river does three kinds of harm. Ammonia is toxic to fish. Bacteria that eat ammonia consume oxygen doing it, so it suffocates a river the way organic matter does. And nitrogen is fertiliser, so downstream, in lakes and estuaries, it grows algae until the algae die, rot, and take the oxygen with them. The dead zones at the mouths of the Mississippi and in the Baltic are made of nitrogen.
Removing it takes two sets of bacteria that want opposite things. One set, given plenty of air, turns ammonia into nitrate. The other, starved of air, turns nitrate into nitrogen gas, which leaves the water and returns to the atmosphere it came from. A modern plant runs both, in tanks side by side, and the gas that bubbles off is the same nitrogen that a fertiliser factory took from the air in the first place.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Membranes
item.description:
The most important piece of equipment in modern water treatment is a sheet of plastic with holes in it too small to imagine.
A membrane is a filter taken to its limit. Sand catches grit. Cloth catches lint. A microfiltration membrane, with pores a tenth of a micron across, catches bacteria. Ultrafiltration, at a hundredth of a micron, catches viruses. Nanofiltration begins to catch dissolved molecules. Reverse osmosis, at the bottom of the scale, holds back salt and lets almost nothing but water through.
Each step down the scale costs more pressure, because pushing water through smaller holes is harder work, and each step catches something the last one could not. A modern reuse plant, in Singapore or in a textile mill in India, is that scale laid out in a row: biology first, then membranes in order of fineness, until what comes out is cleaner than what the city drinks.
The membrane is why water can now be recycled at all. The long version is on the site.
